A firm maintains partners’ capital accounts under the fixed capital method. Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Interest on capital
(B) Partner’s drawings
(C) Additional capital introduced
(D) Share of profit

List-II
(I) Credit side of Partner’s Capital Account
(II) Credit side of Partner’s Current Account
(III) Debit side of Partner’s Current Account

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
candidate.explanation: Under the fixed capital method, items such as interest on capital and share of profit are credited to the Partner’s Current Account, while drawings are debited to it. Additional capital introduced is credited to the Partner’s Capital Account.

reasons: Under the fixed capital method, interest on capital and share of profit are credited to the Current Account (II); drawings are debited to it (III); additional capital is credited to the Capital Account (I). This gives option A.
B misplaces drawings and additional capital; C reverses the interest-on-capital and drawings sides; D misplaces additional capital and share of profit.
There are no numerical inputs or boundary conditions requiring additional assumptions. The empty passage is appropriate for this conceptual matching question.
The question follows the authenticated match-type format and changes the concepts being matched, rather than merely renaming or reshuffling the anchor items.

This includes the amount of money brought in as capital, withdrawal of capital, share of profit, interest on capital, interest on drawings, partner’s salary, commission to partners, etc. There are two methods by which the capital accounts of partners can be maintained. These

are: (i) fixed capital method, and (ii) fluctuating capital method. The difference between the two lies in whether or not the transactions other than addition/withdrawal of capital are recorded in the capital accounts of the partners. (a) Fixed Capital Method: Under the fixed capital method, the capitals of the partners shall remain fixed unless additional capital is introduced or a part of the capital is withdrawn as per the agreement among the partners. All items like share of profit or loss, interest on capital, drawings, interest on drawings, etc. are recorded in a separate accounts, called Partner’s Current Account. The partners’

capital accounts will always show a credit balance, which shall remain the same (fixed) year after year unless there is any addition or withdrawal of capital. The partners’ current account on the other hand, may show a debit or a credit balance. Thus under this method, two accounts are maintained for each partner viz., capital account and current account, While the partners’ capital accounts shall always appear on the liabilities side in the balance sheet, the partners’ current account’s balance shall be shown on the liabilities side, if they have credit balance and on the assets side, if they have debit balance. This includes the amount of money brought in as capital, withdrawal of capital, share of profit, interest on capital, interest on drawings, partner’s salary, commission to partners, etc. There are two methods by which the capital accounts of partners can be maintained. These

are: (i) fixed capital method, and (ii) fluctuating capital method. The difference between the two lies in whether or not the transactions other than addition/withdrawal of capital are recorded in the capital accounts of the partners. (a) Fixed Capital Method: Under the fixed capital method, the capitals of the partners shall remain fixed unless additional capital is introduced or a part of the capital is withdrawn as per the agreement among the partners. All items like share of profit or loss, interest on capital, drawings, interest on drawings, etc. are recorded in a separate accounts, called Partner’s Current Account. The partners’

capital accounts will always show a credit balance, which shall remain the same (fixed) year after year unless there is any addition or withdrawal of capital. The partners’ current account on the other hand, may show a debit or a credit balance. candidate.body: A company forfeited some fully called-up equity shares of ₹10 each. The holders had not paid the final call of ₹3 per share, but the issue premium of ₹2 per share had been received in full. The total amount credited to Share Forfeiture Account on forfeiture was ₹4,200. How many shares were forfeited?

Match List-I with List-II.

List-I

(D) Reserve capital

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
candidate.explanation: Calls in arrears are amounts called on shares but not received, while calls in advance are received before they are due. Securities premium is the amount received above the nominal value of shares. Reserve capital is called at the time of winding up. Thus, the correct matching is (A)–(II), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), and (D)–(III).

reasons: The matches are (A)–(II): calls in arrears are called amounts not received; (B)–(IV): calls in advance are amounts paid before due; (C)–(I): securities premium is the amount above nominal value; and (D)–(III): reserve capital is called at winding up. These pairings appear together only in option D.
The other options misassign at least one of calls in advance, securities premium, or reserve capital.

known as ‘Calls in Advance’ for which a separate account is maintained. This includes the amount of money brought in as capital, withdrawal of capital, share of profit, interest on capital, interest on drawings, partner’s salary, commission to partners, etc. There are two methods by which the capital accounts of partners can be maintained. These

are: (i) fixed capital method, and (ii) fluctuating capital method. The difference between the two lies in whether or not the transactions other than addition/withdrawal of capital are recorded in the capital accounts of the partners. (a) Fixed Capital Method: Under the fixed capital method, the capitals of the partners shall remain fixed unless additional capital is introduced or a part of the capital is withdrawn as per the agreement among the partners. capital accounts will always show a credit balance, which shall remain the same (fixed) year after year unless there is any addition or withdrawal of capital. (A) Trading Account → Profit and Loss Account → Profit and Loss Appropriation Account → Partners’ Capital/Current Accounts → Balance Sheet

(C) Trading Account → Profit and Loss Account → Partners’ Capital/Current Accounts → Profit and Loss Appropriation Account → Balance Sheet
(D) Trading Account → Profit and Loss Account → Profit and Loss Appropriation Account → Balance Sheet → Partners’ Capital/Current Accounts

candidate.body: When a company receives money for a call before the call is made, which journal entry is recorded?
options: Calls in Advance A/c Dr. — To Bank A/c
Bank A/c Dr. — To Calls in Advance A/c
Bank A/c Dr. — To Share Capital A/c
Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. — To Bank A/c
candidate.explanation: The amount received before a call is made is credited to Calls in Advance Account, while Bank Account is debited for the money received.

reasons: Assuming the advance is validly received, the entry is Bank A/c Dr. and Calls in Advance A/c Cr.; the latter is a liability, not share capital (E2.1, E2.2).
A reverses the entry, C credits Share Capital instead of Calls in Advance, and D records calls unpaid rather than received early.
The anchor asks who must authorise acceptance of calls in advance; this asks for the journal entry, so it is meaningfully distinct (E1.1).
This is a direct, syllabus-covered conceptual question. It requires no numerical calculation, and the empty passage does not affect answerability.

supporting_spans.quote: 20. A company can accept calls in advance, if authorised by : (1) Shareholders (2) Board of Directors (3) Articles of Association (4) Memorandum of Association st

18 Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements 1.6.2 Calls in Advance Sometimes shareholders pay a part or the whole of the amount of the calls not yet made. The amount so received from the shareholders is known as “Calls in Advance”. The amount received in advance is a liability of the company and should be credited to ‘Call in Advance Account.” The amount received will be adjusted towards the payment of calls as and when they becomes due. jobs.variant_brief: Use a contrasting case that distinguishes the correct principle from its nearest distractor.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A company offers 20,000 shares to the public and receives valid applications for exactly 20,000 shares. How should the issue be classified?
options: As oversubscribed, because applications have been received for the shares offered.
As undersubscribed, because applications do not exceed the number of shares offered.
As fully subscribed, because applications equal the number of shares offered.
As issued at a premium, because applications equal the number of shares offered.
candidate.explanation: Oversubscription occurs when applications exceed the number of shares offered; undersubscription occurs when applications are fewer. Here, the numbers are equal, so the issue is fully subscribed. The number of applications does not establish whether shares were issued at a premium.

reasons: Applications equal the offer: 20,000 = 20,000. Oversubscription requires applications to exceed the offer, while undersubscription requires fewer applications; equality is full subscription.
Option A is false because there is no excess, B is false because applications are not fewer than shares offered, and D is unrelated: a premium requires an issue price above nominal value.

The equality case asks for a different classification from the anchor’s test of what counts as oversubscription. It is a direct, syllabus-aligned conceptual question. No passage is supplied or needed.

This usually happens in respect of shares issue of well-managed and financially strong companies and is said to be a case of ‘Over Subscription’. For example, a comapny offered 2 lakh shares for subscription to the public but the applications were received for 1,90,000 shares, only. In such a situation, the allotment will be confirmed to 1,90,000 shares and entries shall be made accordingly. However, as stated earlier, it

question.body: A company offers 20,000 shares to the public and receives valid applications for exactly 20,000 shares. How should the issue be classified?
options: As oversubscribed, because applications have been received for the shares offered.
As undersubscribed, because applications do not exceed the number of shares offered.
As fully subscribed, because applications equal the number of shares offered.
As issued at a premium, because applications equal the number of shares offered.
question.explanation: Oversubscription occurs when applications exceed the number of shares offered; undersubscription occurs when applications are fewer. Here, the numbers are equal, so the issue is fully subscribed. The number of applications does not establish whether shares were issued at a premium.

candidate.body: A firm maintains partners’ accounts under the fixed capital method. After all appropriations, a residual profit of ₹1,20,000 is to be shared equally between its two partners. Which journal entry records the transfer of this profit to the partners?
options: Debit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000; credit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000.
Debit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000; credit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000.
Debit Profit and Loss Account ₹1,20,000; credit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000.
Debit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000; credit each partner’s Capital Account ₹60,000.
candidate.explanation: The residual profit is transferred by debiting the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and crediting the partners’ accounts in their profit-sharing proportions. Since the partners share equally, each receives ₹60,000. Under the fixed capital method, this credit is recorded in each partner’s Current Account, not Capital Account.

provenance.adaptation_type: Numerical application of profit allocation under the fixed capital method
Numerical application of profit allocation under the fixed capital method

reasons: Under the fixed capital method, partners’ shares of profit are recorded in their Current Accounts; the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account records distribution of profit.
Equal shares are ₹1,20,000 ÷ 2 = ₹60,000 each. The entry is debit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000 and credit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000.
B reverses the entry, C uses Profit and Loss Account rather than Profit and Loss Appropriation Account, and D credits fixed Capital Accounts instead of Current Accounts.

are: (i) fixed capital method, and (ii) fluctuating capital method. The difference between the two lies in whether or not the transactions other than addition/withdrawal of capital are recorded in the capital accounts of the partners. (a) Fixed Capital Method: Under the fixed capital method, the capitals of the partners shall remain fixed unless additional capital is introduced or a part of the capital is withdrawn as per the agreement among the partners. All items like share of profit or loss, interest on capital, drawings, interest on drawings, etc. are recorded in a separate accounts, called Partner’s Current Account. The partners’

capital accounts will always show a credit balance, which shall remain the same (fixed) year after year unless there is any addition or withdrawal of capital. The partners’ current account on the other hand, may show a debit or a credit balance. Thus under this method, two accounts are maintained for each partner viz., capital account and current account, While the partners’ capital accounts shall always appear on the liabilities side in the balance sheet, the partners’ current account’s balance shall be shown on the liabilities side, if they have credit balance and on the assets side, if they have debit balance. The partner’s capital

commissions are noticed say in respect of the interest on capital, interest on drawings, partner’s salary, commission, etc. necessary adjustments can be made in the partner’s capital accounts through the Profit and Loss Adjustment Account, to rectify the same. 8. Preparation of final accounts of a partnership firm: There is not much difference in the final accounts of a sole proprietary concern and that of a partnership firm except that in case of a partnership firm an additional account called Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is prepared to show distribution of profit and loss among the partners. question.subject: accountancy
question.body: A firm maintains partners’ accounts under the fixed capital method. After all appropriations, a residual profit of ₹1,20,000 is to be shared equally between its two partners. Which journal entry records the transfer of this profit to the partners?
options: Debit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000; credit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000.
Debit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000; credit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000.
Debit Profit and Loss Account ₹1,20,000; credit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000.
Debit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000; credit each partner’s Capital Account ₹60,000.
question.explanation: The residual profit is transferred by debiting the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and crediting the partners’ accounts in their profit-sharing proportions. Since the partners share equally, each receives ₹60,000. Under the fixed capital method, this credit is recorded in each partner’s Current Account, not Capital Account.

candidate.body: Under flexible exchange rate, when the price of domestic currency in terms of foreign currency increases, it is called ___________ .
candidate.explanation: Under a flexible exchange rate, an increase in the price of domestic currency in terms of foreign currency means the domestic currency has gained value. This is called appreciation, so the correct answer is B. Devaluation and revaluation refer to changes made by the government under a fixed exchange rate system.

reasons: A rise in the price of domestic currency in terms of foreign currency is an increase in its value, hence appreciation; option B is correct. A fall in value is depreciation, while devaluation and revaluation are government changes to a fixed exchange rate, so A, C and D do not fit the stated flexible-rate condition.

candidate.body: Identify the correct set of statements. (A) Ex Ante Saving represents what is actually planned to save. (B) Ex Post Saving represents what is actually planned to save. (C) Ex Post Saving depicts what has actually happened. (D) Ex Ante Post Saving represents what is actually saved. Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
candidate.explanation: Ex ante saving is the amount planned to be saved, so statement (A) is correct. Ex post describes what has actually happened, making statement (C) correct. Statement (B) is incorrect because ex post saving is not planned saving; statement (D) is incorrect because “ex ante post saving” is not the term for actual saving. Therefore, the correct answer is (A) and (C) only.

reasons: Ex ante means planned; ex post means what actually happened. Thus (A) and (C) are true, while (B) is false. (D) uses the nonstandard term “Ex Ante Post Saving,” so as written it is false. The correct option is B, (A) and (C) only.
There is no numerical calculation, passage, or relevant boundary case. The item is within income determination and matches the authenticated CUET format.

candidate.body: Which of the following statements are true ? (A) Quantitative tools control the extent of money supply by changing the CRR. (B) There are two types of open market operations – outright and upright. (C) A fall in the bank rate can decrease the money supply. (D) Selling of a bond by RBI leads to reduction in quantity of reserves. (E) The RBI can influence money supply by changing the rate at which it gives loan to the commercial banks. Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
candidate.explanation: Statements (A), (D) and (E) are true. The RBI uses quantitative tools, including changes in the CRR, to influence the extent of money supply. When it sells bonds, buyers pay the RBI, reducing reserves in the banking system and therefore tending to reduce money supply. The RBI can also influence money supply by changing the rate at which it lends to commercial banks. (B) is false: the two types of open market operations are outright and repo, not “outright and upright.” (C) is false: a fall in the bank rate makes borrowing from the RBI cheaper and generally tends to increase, not decrease, money supply. Thus the correct answer is (A), (D) and (E) only.

reasons: A is true: changing CRR is a quantitative tool for controlling money supply. B is false: the two types are outright and repo, not outright and upright. D is true: RBI bond sales reduce reserves.

E is true: changing the rate at which it lends to commercial banks is a way for RBI to influence money supply. Thus only option D lists the true statements.

candidate.body: All those elements which create liability and decrease the assets of government are known as :
candidate.explanation: Capital receipts are government receipts that either create a liability, such as borrowing, or reduce its financial assets, such as proceeds from selling government assets. Therefore, the correct answer is A, Capital Receipts.

reasons: Capital receipts are receipts that create liabilities or reduce the government's financial assets; revenue receipts do not create a claim on government. Capital payments and revenue payments are expenditure categories, so A is the defensible option.

NCERT states the definition with “or,” while the question uses “and”; read as the familiar shorthand describing the two kinds of capital receipts, it points to the same category. The conjunction is imprecise but does not make another option defensible.

candidate.subject: economics
candidate.body: In a two-sector economy consisting only of households and firms, households spend all their income on goods and services produced by domestic firms. There is no saving, government, or external trade, and firms distribute all their sales receipts as factor income. If firms receive ₹720 crore from household purchases during a year, what is the aggregate factor income received by households?
candidate.explanation: In this two-sector circular flow, household expenditure on firms’ output equals firms’ sales receipts. Since firms distribute all those receipts as factor income, household factor income is also ₹720 crore.

reasons: With no saving, government, or external trade, household spending equals firms’ sales revenue; with all sales receipts distributed as factor income, aggregate factor income is ₹720 crore.
Thus A is correct. ₹360 crore and ₹1,440 crore do not match the stated one-for-one circular flow, and ₹0 crore contradicts the distribution of all sales receipts.

The two-sector circular-flow principle is supported by the NCERT excerpts and is within the supplied syllabus. The four-option numerical application is appropriate for the shown CUET format and is substantively distinct from the anchor’s statement-identification task.
The question is self-contained and has no passage-dependent information or unresolved boundary case.

supporting_spans.quote: the capital stock of an economy and thus make production of other commodities possible. 2.2 CIRCULAR FLOW OF INCOME AND METHODS OF CALCULATING NATIONAL INCOME The description of the economy in the previous section enables us to have a rough idea of how a simple economy – without a government, external trade or any savings – may function. The households receive their payments from the firms for productive activities they perform for the latter. As we have mentioned before, there may fundamentally be four kinds of contributions that can be made during the production of goods and services (a) contribution made by human labour, remuneration for

which is called wage (b) contribution made by capital, remuneration for which is called interest (c) contribution made by entrepreneurship, remuneration of which is profit (d) contribution made by fixed natural resources (called ‘land’), remuneration for which is called rent. In this simplified economy, there is only one way in which the households may dispose off their earnings – by spending their entire income on the goods and services produced by the domestic firms. The other channels of disposing their income are closed: we have assumed that the households do not save, they do not pay taxes to the government – since there is no

government, and neither do they buy imported goods since there is no external trade in this simple economy. In other words, factors of production use their remunerations to buy the goods and services which they assisted in producing. The aggregate consumption by the households of the economy is equal to the aggregate expenditure on goods and services produced by the firms in the economy. The Reprint 2026-27

15 1515 1515National Income Accounting entire income of the economy, therefore, comes back to the producers in the form of sales revenue. There is no leakage from the system – there is no difference between the amount that the firms had distributed in the form of factor payments (which is the sum total of remunerations earned by the four factors of production) and the aggregate consumption expenditure that they receive as sales revenue. In the next period the firms will once again produce goods and services and pay remunerations to the factors of production. These remunerations will once again be used to buy the goods and services. Hence year

after year we can imagine the aggregate income of the economy going through the two sectors, firms and households, in a circular way. This is represented in Fig. 2.1. When the income is being spent on the goods and services produced by the firms, it takes the form of aggregate expenditure received by the firms. Since the value of expenditure must be equal to the value of goods and services, we can equivalently measure the aggregate income by “calculating the aggregate value of goods and services pr oduced by the fir ms”. When the aggr egate revenue received by the firms is paid out to the factors of production it takes the form of aggregate

candidate.body: A household plans to consume ₹36,000 and save ₹9,000 during a month. At the end of the month, it has actually consumed ₹39,000 and saved ₹7,000. Assuming disposable income is divided only between consumption and saving, what are its planned disposable income and actual disposable income, respectively?
candidate.explanation: Planned (ex ante) disposable income equals planned consumption plus planned saving: ₹36,000 + ₹9,000 = ₹45,000. Actual (ex post) disposable income equals actual consumption plus actual saving: ₹39,000 + ₹7,000 = ₹46,000.

reasons: Under the stated assumption that disposable income is divided only between consumption and saving, planned disposable income = ₹36,000 + ₹9,000 = ₹45,000; actual disposable income = ₹39,000 + ₹7,000 = ₹46,000. Only option C gives both totals; the other options mismatch at least one.

The distinction between planned and actual values is consistent with the supplied source material on ex ante and ex post measures. The question supplies the allocation assumption needed for the arithmetic.

candidate.body: Under a flexible exchange rate, the foreign-currency price of one unit of domestic currency rises from $0.04 to $0.05. What is the percentage increase in this price, and what does the change indicate?
candidate.explanation: The percentage increase is (($0.05 − $0.04) ÷ $0.04) × 100 = 25%. Under a flexible exchange rate, an increase in the price of domestic currency in terms of foreign currency is an appreciation of the domestic currency.

reasons: The price rises by $0.01 from a base of $0.04, so the percentage increase is ($0.01/$0.04) × 100 = 25%.

Under a flexible exchange rate, an increase in the domestic currency's price in foreign currency indicates appreciation, making B the only correct option. Revaluation applies to a government-set exchange rate, not this flexible-rate change.
The question is within the syllabus and answerable as written. It adds a calculation to the anchor's appreciation concept, making it a substantive numerical variant.

candidate.subject: economics
candidate.body: In a simplified banking system, the required reserve ratio is 20%, banks hold no excess reserves, and there is no cash leakage. Each ₹1 of reserves can therefore support up to ₹5 of bank deposits. After the RBI sells government bonds, the system’s maximum deposit-creation capacity falls by ₹150 crore. Assuming the sale withdraws reserves from banks rupee-for-rupee, what is the value of the bonds sold?
candidate.explanation: A ₹1 reduction in reserves lowers the maximum deposit capacity by ₹5. Therefore, a ₹150 crore reduction in deposit capacity corresponds to a reserve withdrawal—and bond sale proceeds—of ₹150 ÷ 5 = ₹30 crore.

reasons: At a 20% reserve ratio, the deposit multiplier is 1/0.20 = 5; the NCERT example likewise shows ₹100 of reserves supporting ₹500 of deposits (E2.1).

A ₹150 crore fall in maximum deposit capacity therefore corresponds to a reserve withdrawal of ₹150/5 = ₹30 crore. Under the question’s explicit rupee-for-rupee assumption, the bonds sold were worth ₹30 crore (A).
The other choices do not satisfy the stated multiplier: ₹150 crore would imply no multiplication, ₹750 crore reverses the calculation, and ₹7.5 crore gives only a ₹37.5 crore capacity reduction.

NCERT supports the multiplier relationship and that an RBI bond sale reduces reserves and money supply (E2.3, E2.5). All relevant simplifying assumptions, including no excess reserves or cash leakage, are stated; no passage is needed.

The syllabus includes money creation, the money multiplier, and RBI policy tools. Compared with the anchor’s qualitative statement about bond sales reducing reserves, this is a substantive numerical application rather than a cosmetic rewrite (E1.1).

question.body: In a simplified banking system, the required reserve ratio is 20%, banks hold no excess reserves, and there is no cash leakage. Each ₹1 of reserves can therefore support up to ₹5 of bank deposits. After the RBI sells government bonds, the system’s maximum deposit-creation capacity falls by ₹150 crore. Assuming the sale withdraws reserves from banks rupee-for-rupee, what is the value of the bonds sold?
question.explanation: A ₹1 reduction in reserves lowers the maximum deposit capacity by ₹5. Therefore, a ₹150 crore reduction in deposit capacity corresponds to a reserve withdrawal—and bond sale proceeds—of ₹150 ÷ 5 = ₹30 crore.

reasons: At a 20% reserve ratio, the deposit multiplier is 1/0.20 = 5; the NCERT example likewise shows ₹100 of reserves supporting ₹500 of deposits (E2.1).

A ₹150 crore fall in maximum deposit capacity therefore corresponds to a reserve withdrawal of ₹150/5 = ₹30 crore. Under the question’s explicit rupee-for-rupee assumption, the bonds sold were worth ₹30 crore (A).
The other choices do not satisfy the stated multiplier: ₹150 crore would imply no multiplication, ₹750 crore reverses the calculation, and ₹7.5 crore gives only a ₹37.5 crore capacity reduction.

candidate.body: In a simple two-sector economy consisting of households and firms, which of the following describes a real flow in the factor market?
options: Households provide factor services to firms.
Firms provide factor payments to households.
Firms provide final goods and services to households.
Households provide consumption expenditure to firms.
candidate.explanation: In the factor market, households supply factor services, such as labour and capital, to firms. This is a real flow. Factor payments from firms to households are a monetary flow, while goods and consumption expenditure flow between firms and households in the goods market.

reasons: A is the real flow in the factor market: households provide factor services to firms. The textbook identifies this as the lower factor-market flow. (E2.4, E3.4)
B is a monetary factor payment; C is a real flow in the goods market; D is monetary expenditure in the goods market. Thus none competes with A. (E3.3, E3.4)
The question needs no numerical assumptions or boundary-case treatment. Circular flow in a two-sector economy is within the included macroeconomics syllabus.

Compared with the anchor’s generic circular-flow statement question, this requires distinguishing real from monetary flows and the factor market from the goods market; it is more than a cosmetic rewrite. (E1.1)

candidate.subject: business_studies
candidate.body: A government rebate makes electric two-wheelers more affordable. Demand rises, manufacturers increase production, and battery suppliers expand capacity; greater battery availability then encourages further purchases. Which characteristic of the business environment is best illustrated?
candidate.explanation: The example shows several environmental factors influencing one another: the rebate affects demand, which affects manufacturers and suppliers, and expanded battery availability feeds back into demand. This mutual influence illustrates inter-relatedness. Dynamic nature refers more broadly to ongoing change, while uncertainty concerns difficulty predicting future events.

reasons: The sequence links the rebate, increased demand, manufacturers’ production, supplier capacity, and further purchases. This connected influence among environmental elements best illustrates inter-relatedness (E3.1).

Dynamic nature (B) involves change, which occurs here, but the emphasis is on the links among the changes. Uncertainty (C) is not indicated; totality of external forces (D) describes their aggregate, not their interaction (E3.2, E3.3).
No calculation or unstated numerical assumption is needed. The stem is answerable without a passage.

question.body: A government rebate makes electric two-wheelers more affordable. Demand rises, manufacturers increase production, and battery suppliers expand capacity; greater battery availability then encourages further purchases. Which characteristic of the business environment is best illustrated?
question.explanation: The example shows several environmental factors influencing one another: the rebate affects demand, which affects manufacturers and suppliers, and expanded battery availability feeds back into demand. This mutual influence illustrates inter-relatedness. Dynamic nature refers more broadly to ongoing change, while uncertainty concerns difficulty predicting future events.

candidate.body: According to the chapter, since Independence and alongside the Five-Year Plans, the Union Budget came to be regarded as more than a statement of receipts and expenditure. What additional role did it acquire?
options: A yearly statement confined to government receipts and expenditure
An instrument exclusively for approving taxation
A report on only the government’s capital expenditure
candidate.explanation: The chapter states that with the launching of the Five-Year Plans, the budget also became a significant national policy statement, rather than merely a statement of receipts and expenditure.

investment in shares, and loans and advances by the central government to state and union territory governments, PSUs and other parties. Capital expenditure is also categorised as plan and non-plan in the budget documents. Plan capital expenditure, like its revenue counterpart, relates to central plan and central assistance for state and union territory plans. Non-plan capital expenditure covers various general, social and economic services provided by the government. The budget is not merely a statement of receipts and expenditures. Since Independence, with the launching of the Five-Year Plans, it has also become a significant national

policy statement. The budget, it has been argued, reflects and shapes, and is, in turn, shaped by the country’s economic life. Along with the budget, three policy statements are mandated by the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 (FRBMA) 4. The Medium-term Fiscal Policy Statement sets a three- year rolling target for specific fiscal indicators and examines whether revenue expenditure can be financed through revenue receipts on a sustainable basis and how productively capital receipts including market borrowings are being utilised. The Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement sets the priorities of the government in the fiscal area,

candidate.body: Identify the correct statement in the context of Circular Flow of Income in a two sector economy :
options: Household receives factor services from firms.
Household supplies factor services to Government.
candidate.explanation: In the two-sector circular flow, households provide factor services to firms, and firms use those services to produce goods and services. Therefore, statement (3) is correct. Statement (1) reverses the direction of factor services. The simple model excludes government, so statement (4) does not apply. It also assumes households spend their entire income and do not save, so statement (2), which says the household invests while the firm saves, does not describe this model.

reasons: C is correct: firms use factor services to produce goods and services. In the two-sector flow, households supply factor services to firms, so A reverses the direction; B does not describe the stated model; and D introduces a government sector absent from the two-sector economy.
The NCERT account supports the factor-service direction and describes the simple circular-flow model without government or household saving. No numerical assumptions or calculations are needed.

supporting_spans.quote: 25. Identify the correct statement in the context of Circular Flow of Income in a two sector economy : (1) Household receives factor services from firms. (2) Household invests while firm saves. (3) Firms produce goods and services. (4) Household supplies factor services to Government.

The incomes so generated create the capacity to purchase the final consumption goods and thus enable their sale by the business enterprises, the basic object of their production. The households receive their payments from the firms for productive activities they perform for the latter. All these considerations have made "Just Foodie" a complete success and they are able to win over different competitors in the market, and their market share is rising continuously.

candidate.body: Based on the Just Foodie case, what customer benefit is the company seeking by selling its products through grocery stores as well as its own outlets?
options: Customers can find the products at convenient places and when they need them.
Customers receive products with improved taste, quality and packaging.
Customers are persuaded to buy through free gifts and cash-back offers.
Customers are charged a higher price than competing brands.
candidate.explanation: Selling through grocery stores adds outlets where customers can obtain the products. This supports their availability at the right place and time, which is the purpose of physical distribution.
candidate.passage_text: "Just Foodie" is a food chain offering different snacks like chips, biscuits, chocochip cookies, cakes, etc. through their own retail outlets. To make their products available to customers at right time, right place, they are also selling their products to grocery stores in addition to their own outlets. The taste, quality and packing are given utmost care. They are offering good quality, so they are able to charge higher price than their competitors. To increase their sales, they are using different offers like : Free gifts, Cash backs, etc. They are offering discounts to customers on various occasions. All these considerations have made "Just Foodie" a complete success and they are able to win over different competitors in the market, and their market share is rising continuously.

reasons: The passage states that grocery-store distribution is intended to make products available at the right time and place; option A restates that customer benefit. The textbook describes physical distribution as activities that make products available to target customers (E2.1, E3.1).

question.body: Based on the Just Foodie case, what customer benefit is the company seeking by selling its products through grocery stores as well as its own outlets?
options: Customers can find the products at convenient places and when they need them.
Customers receive products with improved taste, quality and packaging.
Customers are persuaded to buy through free gifts and cash-back offers.
Customers are charged a higher price than competing brands.
question.explanation: Selling through grocery stores adds outlets where customers can obtain the products. This supports their availability at the right place and time, which is the purpose of physical distribution.
